query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The superior wear performance of high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is primarily governed by the high density of lattice distortions resulting from their multi‐element solid solution, which impedes dislocation motion and enhances plastic deformation resistance during sliding wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A sputter‐deposited HEA protective coating with a single-phase, high configurational entropy microstructure (i.e., a random multi-element solid solution) that exhibits high lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Prepare a set of comparative coatings by deliberately reducing the level of lattice distortion—for example, by substituting one or more principal elements with an element that has a similar atomic radius but a lower mixing enthalpy, thereby decreasing the degree of lattice strain and configurational disorder.
generation.conditions: Perform standardized ball‐on‐disk wear tests at room temperature in ambient air under controlled load (to invoke adhesive and abrasive wear regimes) and constant sliding speed. Ensure that both the baseline and modified coatings are processed identically apart from the compositional substitution.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale lattice distortions which create obstacles to dislocation motion and thereby modify the plastic deformation mechanisms under wear.
generation.mechanism: In high-entropy alloys, the severe lattice distortions induced by the multiple unsynchronized atomic sizes act to hinder dislocation glide. This leads to an enhanced ability to absorb and dissipate mechanical energy, thereby improving wear resistance. Reducing these distortions by lowering compositional complexity should diminish this mechanism, resulting in higher wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA coating, the modified coating with reduced lattice distortions is expected to exhibit an increased wear volume and more pronounced wear artifacts (such as higher rates of material removal), thus showing deteriorated wear performance.
generation.baseline: The HEA protective coating with a fully random, high-entropy composition and high lattice distortion developed through standard sputter deposition.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for HEA coatings that form stable single-phase solid solutions and are subject to typical sliding wear conditions that do not exceed the thresholds for severe plastic deformation or introduce additional wear mechanisms (e.g., oxidation induced high-temperature wear).
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of lattice distortion and wear resistance is not yet established, and other microstructural features (such as nanograin boundaries) may also contribute to wear performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of coatings: one set with the baseline high-entropy composition (high lattice distortion) and another set where one or more principal elements are replaced to lower the expected lattice distortion. Both sets should be deposited under identical sputtering conditions. Carry out ball‐on‐disk wear tests under identical conditions (e.g., constant normal load, sliding speed, and ambient temperature).
measurements: Quantitative wear volume measurements (e.g., via profilometry)
Microstructural characterization of lattice distortion (e.g., using X-ray diffraction line broadening or high-resolution TEM)
Surface morphology of wear tracks (e.g., SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with intentionally reduced lattice distortions exhibit wear performance (i.e., wear volume and damage morphology) that is statistically indistinguishable from, or better than, that of the baseline high-entropy coatings, the hypothesized role of lattice distortion in governing wear performance would be falsified.
